title: Keeping a quadrotor in the air
summary: Hover thrust, how rotor limits cap a climb, and what a motor failure does to a quadcopter.

steps.title: A quarter of the weight each
steps.text:
To hover, the four rotors together must carry the weight m g, so each one gives m g / 4. Here the quadrotor starts tilted 20° and its controller levels it; on the Rotor thrusts tab every rotor settles on the dotted hover line.

Make the quadrotor heavier: set the Mass to 1.5 kg and run. What does each rotor carry now?

check.success: 1.5 × 9.81 / 4 = 3.68 N per rotor. The thrust-to-weight ratio fell from 2.4 to 1.6: less thrust left over to manoeuvre.

steps.title: Rotors at their limit
steps.text:
This quadrotor's rotors give at most 3.5 N each: a thrust-to-weight ratio of only 1.43. Asked to climb 17 m, the height loop wants far more thrust than that.

Run it and look at the Rotor thrusts tab: the shaded band is where the mixer is saturated. How long does it stay there?

check.success: More than 2 s at full thrust: the climb is limited by the motors, not the controller. Its acceleration is only (4 Tmax − m g) / m ≈ 4.2 m/s².

steps.title: More thrust, faster climb
steps.text: Raise the Rotor thrust limit to 6 N and run again. Watch the Position tab: the climb gets steeper, and the rotors are saturated for less time.

check.success: It settles in about 2 s instead of 3.3 s. The gains did not change: the extra speed came only from the motors.

steps.title: A motor stops
steps.text:
At t = 2 s rotor 1 (front-left) stops. To stay level, the controller must slow rotor 3, its diagonal partner. But rotors 1 and 3 both spin clockwise: now the counter-clockwise pair's drag torque is no longer balanced, and nothing can stop the yaw.

Run it and look at the Attitude tab and the Animation.

check.success: Hundreds of degrees per second. The mixer gives up yaw first, so the spin grows until roll and pitch are lost too, and the quadrotor crashes.

steps.title: A damaged rotor
steps.text: Not every failure is total. Set Thrust left to 0.5 (a chipped propeller) and run. Does it stay in the air?

check.success: It survives: the other rotors make up the lost thrust, and the yaw controller still has enough torque left to hold a slow turn. It drifts, but it flies.
